content: 1. Hall MT, Smith MA, Simms KT, Barnabas R, Canfell K, and Murray JM conducted a modeling study to evaluate the historical, current, and potential future effects of HIV prevention and control measures on HPV and cervical disease in Tanzania. This study was published in PLoS One in 2020, volume 15, issue 5, under the article identifier e0231388. 2. Pfadenhauer LM, Gerhardus A, Mozygemba K, Bakke Lysdahl K, Booth A, Hofmann B, and colleagues developed the Context and Implementation of Complex Interventions (CICI) framework. This framework aims to address the intricacies of context and implementation in complex interventions. Their work was published in Implementation Science in 2017, volume 12, issue 1, spanning pages 1–17, with the DOI 10.1186/s13012-017-0552-5. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides public reports on prequalified in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), including those for HPV testing. These reports are accessible through the WHO diagnostics laboratory evaluations website. 4. The WHO has published a document titled Cervical Cancer: Screening and Treatment of Pre-cancerous Lesions for Secondary Prevention of Cervical Cancer, which outlines the technological landscape for addressing cervical cancer prevention. 5. WHO technical guidance and specifications for medical devices used in the screening and treatment of precancerous cervical lesions have been made available in a detailed PDF document. This guidance supports the prevention of cervical cancer. 6. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) published monographs evaluating the carcinogenic risks of biological agents to humans. Volume 100B, released in 2012, focuses on these evaluations and is a critical resource for understanding cancer risks. 7. The WHO's consolidated guideline on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and service delivery, now in its third edition, provides recommendations based on a public health approach. This guideline was published in Geneva in 2021. 8. The United Nations Joint Global Programme on Cervical Cancer Prevention involves collaboration between WHO, IAEA, IARC, UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNICEF, and UN Women. This program aims to address cervical cancer prevention comprehensively. 9. WHO has outlined a nine-step strategy for developing scaling-up plans for health interventions. This strategy is detailed in a publication available on the WHO reproductive health website. 10. A WHO publication titled Beginning with the End in Mind provides guidance on planning pilot projects and programmatic research to ensure successful scaling-up of health interventions. 11. Practical guidance for scaling up health service innovations is available through a WHO publication, which provides strategic approaches for implementing health innovations effectively. 12. The concept of living guidelines has been introduced by WHO to ensure global recommendations remain up-to-date. This approach is particularly relevant to maternal and perinatal health and was discussed in BMJ Global Health in 2019, volume 4, issue 4, under the article identifier e001683. 13. Annex 1 of the WHO guideline document lists the members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), including co-chairs Julie Torode and Mike Chirenje, and provides details about their affiliations and areas of expertise. 14. The modeling team supporting the development of these guidelines was led by Karen Canfell at the Daffodil Centre, a joint venture between the University of Sydney and Cancer Council NSW. The team utilized the Policy1-Cervix platform to model the impact of interventions on women in the general population and those living with HIV. 15. The systematic review team, led by Marc Arbyn of the Belgian Cancer Centre, contributed evidence on HPV triage strategies, which informed the modeling work. This team included experts from various institutions and countries. 16. The WHO Secretariat, based in Geneva, Switzerland, and regional advisors from WHO and IARC, provided technical and administrative support for the guideline development process. Their contributions spanned multiple departments, including noncommunicable diseases, immunization, sexual and reproductive health, and global HIV programs. 17. Observers and external reviewers, including representatives from international organizations such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, USAID, and Unitaid, participated in the guideline review process to ensure comprehensive and inclusive recommendations. 18. Annex 2 of the guideline document details the evidence-gathering teams and task groups responsible for defining outcomes, eligibility criteria for ablation or referral, and clinical algorithms. These teams were led by experts such as Partha Basu, Maribel Almonte, and Ruanne Barnabas.
